subject: mathematics
question_text: Define the inverse of a matrix.

mark_split.label: Give the condition and an example

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.36, chapter 5 MATRICES, Very Short Answer question 23. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 split rewards the definition AB = BA = I separately from the existence condition det A ≠ 0 with a worked example, because a definition that omits the condition describes something that need not exist. recall_prompt: Say the definition of the inverse, and say when it exists.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: State the definition
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both products are needed: AB = I and BA = I. Write the order n once, because the inverse is defined only for square matrices.
lines: Let A be a square matrix of order n. If there is
a square matrix B of the same order such that
AB = BA = I, where I is the unit matrix of
order n, then B is called the inverse of A.

recall.must_convey: That B is the inverse of the square matrix A when AB = BA = I, and that it is written A⁻¹.
accept: B is the inverse of A if A B equals B A equals the unit matrix
the inverse multiplied either way gives the identity
it is written A to the power minus one
A B equals B A equals I aithe B is A inverse
both products with the inverse give the unit matrix

steps.why: Both products are written because matrix multiplication does not commute in general, so AB = I alone is a weaker statement. For square matrices of the same order the two conditions turn out to be equivalent, but the definition states both.
common_mistakes: Writing A⁻¹ = 1/A, which has no meaning for matrices.
Giving only AB = I and leaving out BA = I.
Defining an inverse for a matrix that is not square.
steps.memory_tip: Inverse means the product either way is the unit matrix: AB = BA = I.

steps.label: Give the condition and an example
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The condition det A ≠ 0 is part of the answer, not an afterthought. A singular matrix has no inverse at all.
lines: A⁻¹ exists if and only if det A ≠ 0, that is
only when A is non-singular. It is then unique,

lines.text: ∴ AB = BA = I means B = A⁻¹, det A ≠ 0

recall.must_convey: That A⁻¹ exists if and only if det A ≠ 0, that it is unique, and that A⁻¹ = (Adj A)/(det A).
accept: the inverse exists if and only if the determinant is not zero
only a non singular matrix has an inverse
A inverse equals adjoint of A divided by determinant of A
determinant zero kaakapothe ne inverse untundi
the inverse is unique when it exists

steps.why: The determinant sits in the denominator of A⁻¹ = (Adj A)/(det A), so a zero determinant leaves nothing to divide by. That is why the condition belongs inside the definition rather than being added later.
common_mistakes: Saying every square matrix has an inverse.
Writing A⁻¹ = (det A)/(Adj A), with the two the wrong way round.
Giving an example whose determinant is 0.
steps.memory_tip: No inverse without a non-zero determinant, because det A is the divisor in (Adj A)/(det A).
